title: Back to Bethel: Promises Renewed, Rachel and Isaac Die
summary: God sends Jacob back to Bethel, and Jacob has his household give up their foreign gods, which he buries before they go. At Bethel God appears to him again, confirms the name Israel, and renews the promises of descendants, kings, and land. On the road south Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin, Reuben sleeps with his father's concubine, and Jacob reaches his father Isaac at Hebron, where Isaac dies and is buried by his two sons.
story: After the disaster at Shechem (chapter 34), God speaks for the first time since Jacob arrived back in Canaan, and he sends Jacob to the place where his years away began. At Bethel, some twenty years before, Jacob vowed that if God brought him home safely, the LORD would be his God and the stone would become God's house (28:20-22). This chapter is the keeping of that vow and the close of Jacob's own story as the main character. It ties off loose ends: the household gods are buried, the name Israel is confirmed, the twelfth son is born, the twelve are listed, and Isaac dies. From chapter 37 on, the focus moves to Jacob's sons, above all Joseph. Grief runs through the chapter, with three deaths in twenty-nine verses, but so does promise. God's words in verses 11-12 gather up the blessings of Genesis: fruitfulness from creation, nations and kings from the covenant with Abraham, and the land.
historical:
Jacob's route runs from Shechem south along the ridge road through the hill country: to Bethel, then toward Ephrath, then past the Tower of Eder to Hebron. Hebron, also called Kiriath-arba, lay in the Judean hills about twenty miles south of Jerusalem, near Mamre, where Abraham had camped and where he bought the cave of Machpelah as a family tomb (chapter 23). The family's center returns to the place of Abraham's grave.

The site of Rachel's tomb is a real historical question. This chapter places it on the way to Ephrath, which a note identifies with Bethlehem, and a traditional tomb at the northern edge of Bethlehem has been honored for many centuries. But 1 Samuel 10:2 puts Rachel's tomb “in Zelzah on the border of Benjamin,” north of Jerusalem, and Jeremiah hears Rachel weeping in Ramah, also in Benjamin's territory (Jeremiah 31:15). Some scholars think Ephrath here names a district near Benjamin's border and the Bethlehem note reflects a later identification; others hold that Ephrath and Bethlehem are the same place and the tomb lay near it. The promise that kings would come from Jacob (verse 11) found its first fulfillment in Saul, from the tribe of the son born in this chapter, and then in David of Judah.
cultural:
Giving up foreign gods, washing, and changing clothes were acts of preparation before meeting God, the outward sign of a household changing its loyalty (compare Exodus 19:10, where Israel washes its clothes before Sinai). The earrings buried with the idols were probably amulets or ornaments tied to other gods. Burying them under a great tree near Shechem was a way of leaving them behind for good, and centuries later Joshua called Israel to the same decision at the same city: “get rid of the foreign gods among you” (Joshua 24:23).

Two more customs appear later in the chapter. A drink offering, wine or another liquid poured out before God, is mentioned here for the first time in the Bible, poured on the pillar along with oil. And Reuben's act with Bilhah was more than lust. In the ancient Near East, taking a ruler's concubine was a claim to his place. Absalom did it publicly to declare his revolt against David (2 Samuel 16:21-22), and Solomon treated Adonijah's request for David's companion Abishag as a bid for the throne (1 Kings 2:13-25). Reuben, the firstborn, seems to be seizing his father's authority early.
literary: The chapter is a closing frame. Bethel opened Jacob's years away (chapter 28) and Bethel closes them, and the language deliberately repeats: God appears, Jacob sets up a pillar, anoints it with oil, and names the place Bethel. God's words in verse 10 repeat the renaming at the Jabbok, now spoken plainly in daylight, and verse 11 echoes both the first blessing of creation, “Be fruitful and multiply” (1:28), and the promise to Abraham that “kings will descend from you” (17:6). The last part of the chapter reads like the end of a book: three deaths (Deborah, Rachel, Isaac), the twelve sons listed by their mothers, and Isaac's death rounding off the section Genesis introduced as the account of Isaac (25:19). By the chronology Genesis gives elsewhere, Isaac actually lived about a dozen years after Joseph was sold (compare 25:26; 37:2; 41:46; 45:6; 47:9), so his death is placed here to finish one generation's story before the next begins. Hebrew manuscripts also mark a paragraph break in the middle of verse 22, right after Reuben's act, as if the text itself falls silent.

doctrines.note: Before going up to Bethel, Jacob's household hands over its foreign gods, washes, and changes clothes. Turning to God involves turning from his rivals, concretely and together, not only in private feeling.

God confirms to Jacob the name Israel and the promises first made to Abraham and Isaac: fruitfulness, a nation and a company of nations, kings, and the land. The covenant has passed intact to the third generation, and God speaks of the land as a gift already given and still to be given.

The chapter sets God's renewed promise beside three graves and a family scandal. Blessing in Genesis doesn't exempt the blessed from grief. Rachel dies bearing the son who completes the twelve, and the promise goes on through her loss.

words.note: Nekhar, foreign, belonging to another people. The foreign gods (verses 2, 4) are the gods of other nations, presumably including the household gods Rachel brought from Haran (31:19). The phrase returns at turning points in Israel's history when the people are called to choose the LORD alone (Joshua 24:23; 1 Samuel 7:3).

Benjamin, son of the right hand. The dying Rachel names her son Ben-oni, usually understood as son of my sorrow, though the word can also mean strength. Jacob renames him Benjamin, and in the Bible the right hand stands for strength, favor, and honor. Jacob refuses to let his last son carry a name of grief.

Nesekh, drink offering, a liquid (usually wine) poured out before God. This is its first appearance in the Bible (verse 14). The law later prescribes drink offerings with the daily sacrifices (Numbers 28:7), and Paul uses the image for his own life being spent for others (Philippians 2:17; 2 Timothy 4:6).

christ: Matthew connects Rachel's grief with the birth of Jesus. When Herod killed the young boys of Bethlehem, Matthew quoted Jeremiah: “A voice is heard in Ramah, weeping and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more” (Matthew 2:18). Rachel, who died in childbirth on the road to Bethlehem, becomes the mother who weeps for Israel's lost children, and Jeremiah's next lines promise that her children will come back (Jeremiah 31:16). The promise that “kings shall descend from you” (verse 11) runs through David to the one Matthew calls the son of David. Benjamin's line produced King Saul and, much later, Saul of Tarsus, who called himself a man “of the tribe of Benjamin” (Philippians 3:5) and became the apostle who carried the promise to Abraham far beyond Israel. Some Christians have also seen in the change from Ben-oni to Benjamin a picture of Christ, the man of sorrows now at God's right hand. That is an association the text doesn't claim, but it matches the shape of the gospel.

hard.q: Why does Genesis report Reuben's sin with Bilhah and then say nothing more?
hard.a:
Verse 22 tells of Reuben's act in a single sentence and adds only that Israel heard about it. There is no confrontation, no punishment, no comment. Some readers see this silence as another sign of Jacob's passivity as a father, the same silence he kept when Dinah was violated (34:5). Others think the narrator is holding the matter for its proper moment, which comes on Jacob's deathbed: “you will no longer excel, because you went up to your father's bed” (49:4). Chronicles later says Reuben's birthright passed to the sons of Joseph because of it (1 Chronicles 5:1). Some rabbinic interpreters, uneasy with the plain sense, read the verse as Reuben disturbing his father's bed to defend his mother Leah's place after Rachel's death, but most readers take the words as they stand.

The act was probably a power play as much as a sexual sin, a firstborn grabbing for his father's authority too soon and losing it. The brevity of the report is part of its force. Genesis records the sins of Israel's founders without dwelling on them and without covering them, and the chapter that renews God's promises also records how unworthy the heirs of those promises were.

questions: Jacob's household gave up their foreign gods before going to meet God. What would it mean for you to set something aside before drawing near to God?
Rachel named her son out of sorrow, and Jacob renamed him in hope. How can faith reframe a loss without denying it?
God renewed his promises to Jacob in a chapter full of graves. How have God's promises and real grief belonged together in your own experience?
